title: The Charli
hook: TikTok’s biggest star already drank Dunkin’. So Dunkin’ put her order on the menu.
situation: Charli D’Amelio was the most followed person on TikTok, and her fans had seen her with a Dunkin’ cup in her videos for months. Dunkin’ wanted younger customers, and more of them using its app.
exchange: Dunkin’ named her usual order, cold brew with whole milk and three pumps of caramel swirl, ‘The Charli’. She promoted it to her followers.
brought: A national menu, its app and thousands of shops.
Tens of millions of young followers and a genuine habit.
turning_point: The Charli launched in September 2020. On launch day Dunkin’ app downloads jumped 57% on the previous 90-day average, and the company later said it had sold hundreds of thousands of the drink in five days.
metric_label: Dunkin’ app downloads on launch day
measure: Compared with the previous 90-day average, as reported by Dunkin’. Cold brew sales rose 20% on day one and 45% on day two
evidence: The figures come from Dunkin’ itself and weren’t independently audited. They are unusually direct, because the drink was only sold under her name.
lesson: The best creator partnership starts with something the creator already does. Turn a real habit into a product, and the fans will order it.
take: Nobody had to pretend. Charli already ordered it, so the partnership just put a name on her cup.
announcement: Read the launch story · Marketing Dive

title: Make It Count
place: New York, then around the world
hook: Nike gave a filmmaker a budget for an advert. He spent it travelling the world.
situation: Nike wanted a film about its FuelBand activity tracker and the line ‘Make it count’. Casey Neistat was a New York filmmaker with a growing YouTube following.
exchange: Nike paid for the film. Neistat ignored the brief and spent the budget on a ten-day trip around the world with his friend Max, filming as he went.
brought: A production budget and a slogan.
A personal style of filmmaking and an online audience.
turning_point: Released in 2012, the film showed the trip rather than the product, and Nike let it run. It was viewed more than 1.5 million times in three days.
metric_label: Views in the first three days
measure: Reported views at launch. The film has since passed 30 million views. Views measure reach, not FuelBand sales
evidence: The views are well documented, and the film helped launch Neistat’s career as one of YouTube’s biggest creators. Nike published no figure for its effect on sales.
lesson: When you hire a creator for their voice, let them use it. The brief can kill what made them worth hiring.
take: The moment brands learned that the creator might know the audience better than the agency. Nike’s best decision was saying yes to something it hadn’t asked for.

creative.label: Watch ‘Make It Count’ on Casey Neistat’s channel

announcement: Read the story · The Daily Meal

title: Built on YouTube
hook: A teenager’s gym clothes company grew by sending its products to YouTubers.
situation: Ben Francis started Gymshark in Birmingham in 2012, while delivering pizzas. It had no budget for advertising, but fitness YouTubers were becoming famous.
exchange: Gymshark sent its clothes to fitness creators such as Lex Griffin and Nikki Blackketter, who wore them in their videos. The creators got clothes, and later fees, and Gymshark got credibility with their audiences.
brought: Clothes made for the gym, and a founder who was part of the scene.
Audiences who trusted what they wore.
turning_point: Gymshark built its brand on creator partnerships rather than advertising. In August 2020 General Atlantic bought a 21% stake, valuing the company at more than £1bn.
measure: The value implied by General Atlantic’s investment. A deal term, not a measure of the creator partnerships
evidence: The valuation is documented, but it can’t be separated into what creators contributed. The early partnerships are told mostly by the founder.
lesson: Partner with creators before they’re famous, and grow together. Early belief buys loyalty that later money can’t.
take: Gymshark didn’t buy influence. It was part of a community and grew up with it.
credit: Gymshark and its early creators, from 2012
impact_source: Read about the valuation · BBC News

title: Girl Online
hook: A YouTuber’s first novel outsold every debut on record, and then the questions started.
situation: Zoe Sugg, known as Zoella, was one of Britain’s biggest YouTubers, with millions of teenage followers. Penguin wanted to reach readers who watched more than they read.
exchange: Penguin published a young adult novel under her name. Zoella promoted it to her audience.
brought: Millions of young followers who trusted her.
turning_point: Girl Online sold 78,109 copies in its first week in November 2014, a record for a debut author. Days later Penguin confirmed she had not written it on her own, and that an editorial consultant had worked on it.
metric_label: Copies sold in the first week, a debut record
measure: Nielsen BookScan’s first-week sales for the UK, the highest for a debut since its records began in 1998
evidence: Book sales are independently tracked, which makes this one of the cleaner figures in the edition. The ghostwriting revelation led to a backlash, but the sales were already made.
lesson: Be honest about who did what. An audience that trusts a creator feels it most when the work isn’t what it seems.
take: The sales proved the audience was real. The backlash proved it cared about authenticity more than publishers expected.

title: To Apple, Love Taylor
hook: One open letter changed Apple’s policy overnight.
situation: Apple was about to launch Apple Music with a free three-month trial, during which it planned not to pay artists. Taylor Swift had the year’s biggest album, 1989.
exchange: Apple needed artists to license their music. Swift could give or withhold the most wanted album of the year.
brought: A new streaming service and hundreds of millions of devices.
Her catalogue and the attention of the industry.
turning_point: On 21 June 2015 Swift posted an open letter saying she would hold back 1989 because artists weren’t paid during the trial. Within about a day, Apple’s Eddy Cue said Apple would pay artists during the trial.
metric_label: Between the letter and Apple changing its policy
measure: About 20 hours, as reported at the time. A fact, not a result
evidence: The letter and Apple’s change are well documented. 1989 later came to Apple Music, and Swift went on to appear in its adverts, but neither side published what the partnership was worth.
lesson: On a platform, the partner with the content has power. Platforms need the work more than any single launch needs the platform.
take: The fastest negotiation in the archive, done in public. Swift showed that a creator can set the terms for a platform.

title: The Restaurant as a Gym
hook: A game sent players to real restaurants, and McDonald’s paid to be the destination.
situation: Pokémon Go was the biggest mobile game of 2016, sending players to real places to catch Pokémon. It launched late in Japan, Pokémon’s home.
exchange: McDonald’s Japan paid to become the game’s first sponsor. About 3,000 restaurants became gyms or PokéStops, places players needed to visit.
brought: Thousands of restaurants and a sponsorship fee.
turning_point: The game launched in Japan on 22 July 2016 with McDonald’s inside it. Reports of the deal sent McDonald’s Japan’s shares up sharply, and July sales rose.
measure: Reported by the company, which credited both Pokémon Go and its Pokémon toys. Other causes are not separated out
evidence: The sales rise and the share price jump are reported, but McDonald’s Japan was also running Pokémon Happy Meal toys and recovering from a food safety crisis.
lesson: When a platform controls where people go, being on the map is worth paying for. Buy the location players need, not just the screen they see.
take: The first sponsored location in a game, and the purest version of the idea: the game sent people through the door.
credit: Niantic, The Pokémon Company and McDonald’s Japan, 2016
links: Read about the share price · NBC News

title: The Infinity Gauntlet
hook: For one week, a film’s villain was inside the world’s biggest game.
situation: Fortnite had become a cultural phenomenon with millions of daily players. Marvel was releasing Avengers: Infinity War, its biggest film yet.
exchange: Marvel let Epic Games put Thanos and the Infinity Gauntlet into Fortnite. Fortnite gave the film a place where its audience already spent its time.
brought: Thanos and the biggest film of the year.
turning_point: The Infinity Gauntlet mode launched on 8 May 2018. Whoever found the gauntlet became Thanos. It set a pattern for film, music and brand events inside Fortnite.
metric_label: How long the mode ran in May 2018
measure: The length of the event. A fact, not a result
evidence: Neither side published what the event did for players or ticket sales. Its significance is what followed: concerts and crossovers became a regular part of Fortnite.
lesson: A game can be a stage for other brands. Fit the partner into how the game is played, not just how it looks.
take: This is where games became media. A film didn’t just advertise in a game, it became part of it.

creative.label: Watch ‘Infinity Gauntlet Limited Time Mashup’ on Fortnite’s channel

impact_source: Read the report · The Next Web

title: New Coke Returns
hook: Coca-Cola brought back its most famous mistake for a show set in 1985.
situation: The third season of Stranger Things was set in the summer of 1985, the year Coca-Cola launched New Coke and withdrew it after 79 days. The show’s creators suggested bringing it back.
exchange: Netflix put New Coke into the story. Coca-Cola made a limited run of the 1985 formula and promoted the season.
brought: One of its biggest shows and a story set in 1985.
Its marketing, and a famous failure people remembered.
turning_point: In May 2019 Coca-Cola announced it would make fewer than 500,000 cans of New Coke for the season, sold through pop-up machines, online and at its Atlanta museum.
metric_label: Cans of New Coke made for the launch
measure: The size of the limited run, announced by Coca-Cola. A fact, not a result
evidence: The partnership and the limited run are documented. Neither company published sales or viewing effects.
lesson: A brand confident enough to joke about its failures can turn them into content. Let the partner tell the story you couldn’t.
take: Brand Turning Points told how New Coke failed in 1985. Thirty-four years later, a streaming show turned it into nostalgia.
links: Read New Coke in Brand Turning Points

title: The Exclusive
hook: Microsoft paid the world’s biggest streamer to move platforms. The platform closed within a year.
situation: Tyler Blevins, known as Ninja, was the most famous streamer on Twitch, with millions of followers watching him play Fortnite. Microsoft’s Mixer was a distant competitor.
exchange: Microsoft paid Ninja a reported $20m to $30m to stream only on Mixer. Ninja was expected to bring his audience with him.
brought: Money and a platform that needed viewers.
turning_point: Ninja moved in August 2019. Many of his viewers didn’t follow, and in June 2020 Microsoft announced it was closing Mixer. Ninja returned to Twitch.
metric_label: From Ninja’s move to the closure announcement
measure: The time between August 2019 and June 2020. A fact, not a result
evidence: The move, the reported fee and the closure are documented. Mixer’s viewing figures weren’t published in full, so how many fans followed him is unclear.
lesson: An audience follows habits, not just people. Paying a creator to move doesn’t move the people who watch them.
take: The creator did well and the platform didn’t. Audiences are loyal to people, but they live on platforms.
impact_source: Read about the closure · Video Games Chronicle
deal_value: Reported at $20m to $30m, from a talent agency’s account

title: Dreams
data_source: A man’s skateboard, a brand’s juice
hook: A man skated to work drinking cranberry juice, and a brand caught up with him.
situation: In September 2020 Nathan Apodaca’s car broke down, so he longboarded to work, drinking Ocean Spray and miming to Fleetwood Mac’s ‘Dreams’. He posted it on TikTok.
exchange: Apodaca made the most shared video of the moment, without being asked. Ocean Spray gave him a new truck filled with juice.
brought: A truck, and the sense to join in rather than take over.
A video millions of people loved.
turning_point: The video went viral within days. Ocean Spray surprised Apodaca with a cranberry red truck, Mick Fleetwood made his own version, and ‘Dreams’ had its biggest streaming week ever.
metric_label: US streams of ‘Dreams’ in a week, per Billboard
measure: The song’s largest streaming week, reported by Billboard. It shows Fleetwood Mac’s gain, not Ocean Spray’s
evidence: The streams are tracked independently, but they belong to the band. Ocean Spray didn’t publish a sales effect.
lesson: Sometimes the partner finds you. When a customer makes something great with your product, reward them quickly and don’t try to own it.
take: Ocean Spray didn’t write the brief, cast the star or pick the song. Its only job was to say thank you, and it did that well.

creative.label: Watch ‘Nathan Apodaca Truck Surprise’ on Ocean Spray’s channel

title: The First Roblox Concert
data_source: Roblox’s players, Lil Nas X’s new single
hook: A rapper performed inside a children’s game, and 33 million views followed.
situation: During the pandemic, live concerts stopped. Lil Nas X had broken through on TikTok, and Roblox had tens of millions of young daily players.
exchange: Lil Nas X performed as a motion-captured avatar and premiered a new single. Roblox gave him an audience his age and a new way to perform.
brought: Tens of millions of young players and a virtual stage.
Lil Nas X and Columbia Records
A star and a new single.
turning_point: Over the weekend of 14 and 15 November 2020, Lil Nas X performed four shows in Roblox, including the debut of ‘Holiday’.
metric_label: Views across the four shows, as reported
measure: Views reported after the weekend. A view is not a unique visitor, and Roblox didn’t publish unique attendance
evidence: The views are a reach figure. Neither side published what the concert did for streams of the single or for Roblox.
lesson: Go where the audience already is, in a form that suits the place. A concert in a game should feel like part of the game.
take: A musician met fans in their own playground. The audience didn’t have to come to him.
credit: Roblox, Lil Nas X and Columbia Records, 2020

creative.label: Watch ‘The Lil Nas X Full Roblox Concert’ on Lil Nas X’s channel

title: MrBeast Burger
hook: The biggest YouTuber in the world opened hundreds of restaurants in a day, without building any.
situation: Jimmy Donaldson, known as MrBeast, had one of YouTube’s largest audiences. Virtual Dining Concepts ran delivery-only brands cooked in existing restaurants’ kitchens.
exchange: MrBeast licensed his name and promoted the brand. Virtual Dining Concepts arranged for restaurants to cook and deliver the burgers.
brought: Kitchens in hundreds of existing restaurants.
His name and an enormous young audience.
turning_point: MrBeast Burger launched in December 2020 with about 300 locations and grew quickly. In 2023 MrBeast sued to end the deal, saying the food quality damaged his reputation. Virtual Dining Concepts sued him back.
metric_label: Locations on launch day, as reported
measure: The number of kitchens at launch. A fact, not a sales figure
evidence: The launch and the lawsuits are on the record. Sales were never published, and the dispute was about quality, not demand.
lesson: If your name is the product, control the quality. A licence can scale faster than you can check it.
take: The audience turned up. The burgers didn’t always live up to the name, and that hurt the creator more than the kitchen.
announcement: Read about the lawsuit · Restaurant Business
impact_source: Read about the countersuit · NBC News

brand: Animal Crossing × Valentino and Marc Jacobs
title: Lockdown Couture
hook: With shops shut, fashion houses dressed people inside a game.
situation: In spring 2020, lockdown closed shops and Animal Crossing: New Horizons became one of the games of the year. Players were designing their own clothes in the game.
exchange: Valentino and Marc Jacobs released in-game versions of their real collections, through a fan-run Instagram account. Players could download and wear them free.
brought: Time, attention and a love of dressing up.
turning_point: In May 2020 Marc Jacobs released six looks and Valentino twenty, drawn from their spring and pre-fall collections. Other designers followed.
metric_label: Looks released by the two houses
measure: Six from Marc Jacobs and twenty from Valentino. A fact, not a result
evidence: The releases are documented. The designs were free, and neither house published any effect on sales or awareness.
lesson: When the usual channels close, go where people are spending time. A game can be a showroom.
take: The most charming case here. Nobody paid, nobody sold anything, and it still felt like a turning point for fashion in games.
credit: Valentino, Marc Jacobs and the Animal Crossing Fashion Archive, 2020

title: Gucci Garden
hook: A virtual handbag resold for more than the real one.
situation: Gucci wanted to reach young people years before they could afford its products. Roblox had over 40 million daily users, many of them children and teenagers.
exchange: Gucci built a virtual exhibition inside Roblox and sold limited digital items. Roblox gave Gucci a young audience and a new kind of product.
brought: Its designs, its name and a virtual exhibition.
Tens of millions of young players and a virtual economy.
turning_point: In May 2021, during the two-week Gucci Garden event, a digital Dionysus bag that had sold for about $6 resold for 350,000 Robux, about $4,115, more than the real bag.
metric_label: Resale price of a virtual Gucci bag, as reported
measure: One resale reported in May 2021. The price later fell sharply. A demand signal, not Gucci’s revenue
evidence: The resale price was widely reported but came from a single sale, and the bag’s value later dropped. Gucci published no revenue or brand figures.
lesson: Digital goods can carry real status. Scarcity works online as well as in a shop, if the brand means something.
take: A child could own Gucci for the price of a sandwich. That might be the most important customer Gucci met all year.

creative.label: Watch ‘Archetypes | Gucci Garden Virtual Exhibition’ on Roblox’s channel

title: Prime Hydration
data_source: Two creators’ audiences, a drinks company
hook: Two rival YouTubers launched a drink, and children queued outside shops for it.
situation: Logan Paul and KSI had fought each other in boxing matches watched by millions. With the drinks company Congo Brands, they launched a sports drink in 2022.
exchange: Paul and KSI promoted Prime to their audiences. Congo Brands made and distributed it.
turning_point: Prime sold out across Britain and America, with bottles resold for many times their price. By 2024 sales were falling fast, and a bottler sued Prime, saying it cut ties when demand collapsed.
metric_label: Fall in Prime’s UK revenue in a year, as reported
measure: A decline of more than 70% reported from company figures. Earlier sales claims came from the founders and weren’t audited
evidence: The rise and fall are documented, and the lawsuits put some figures on the record. The steepest claims about early sales came from the founders themselves.
lesson: An audience can launch a product. Keeping it on shelves takes a reason to buy again.
take: The most dramatic sales curve in the archive. Hype brought people in once, the drink had to bring them back, and it struggled.
credit: Logan Paul, KSI and Congo Brands, 2022
announcement: Read about the sales fall · Business Insider
impact_source: Read about the lawsuit · Bloomberg Law
